passage: Six-year-old Vaibhav sat on the doorstep holding Nani's shawl. "Who will tell me the crocodile story now?" he asked. His mother, Bidisha, said, "Nani has died, and she cannot come back. I miss her too." He asked again the next morning, and she answered again in the same plain words. On Sunday the house filled with relatives. Aunties chopped vegetables in the kitchen, uncles sat on the floor reading prayers, and some people cried while others passed around tea. His father, Tejas, carried in a big pot of rice. Vaibhav did not follow the words, but he leaned against his uncle's arm and stayed. Later he found the photo album and stopped at Dada, who had died the winter before and used to keep toffees in his pocket for him. "Dada gave me sweets," he said, smiling and wiping his eyes. Bidisha helped him draw Dada holding a giant toffee. That night, in the dark, he whispered, "Mummy, will you die too?" Bidisha lay down beside him. "Everybody dies one day, but most people live a very long time. Papa and I are here, and we will always look after you." He held her hand until he fell asleep.

qa.q: What was Vaibhav holding when he sat on the doorstep?
How did Vaibhav's feelings at night differ from what he felt looking at Dada's photo, and what helped each?
qa.a: Looking at Dada's photo he felt warm and sad together, and drawing Dada with a toffee helped; at night he was frightened and asked if Mummy would die, and calm honest words that most people live a long time helped.

qa.q: What might Vaibhav have been feeling when he whispered his question in the dark?
qa.a: He was probably frightened; he asked in the dark and held Bidisha's hand until he fell asleep.

qa.q: Which choice by Bidisha helped Vaibhav with his grief, and why?
qa.a: She answered his repeated questions in the same plain words, so he could ask again and feel safe and looked after.

grounding: A young child's grief for a grandparent, his night-time fear, a warm memory of another grandparent, and the family gathering that holds him.
